slides.title: What Is a Computer Network?
slides.lead: A computer network connects two or more devices so they can share data and resources using agreed rules called protocols.
paragraphs: Computers, phones, servers, and network printers join together over wired Ethernet cables or wireless radio links so they can communicate reliably.
Once connected, devices send and interpret messages using shared communication rules, allowing users to share files, messages, and printers even without Internet access.

slides.title: Five Elements of Data Communication
slides.lead: Every network exchange requires five elements: a sender, receiver, message, medium, and protocol.
items: Sender: The device or computer that creates and starts sending a message—such as your laptop opening a webpage or a phone sending a chat.
Receiver: The target device meant to get and read the message, such as a friend’s smartphone, a shared office printer, or a web server.
Message: The actual information being sent across the network, whether it is text, a photo, an email, a print job, or a video stream.
Medium: The physical pathway (copper Ethernet cable or glass optical fiber) or wireless radio waves carrying signals from sender to receiver.
Protocol: The shared rulebook for formatting, addressing, sending, and checking messages so both devices speak the same digital language.

slides.title: Uses and Importance of Networking
slides.lead: Computer networks improve everyday communication, resource sharing, centralized storage, and team collaboration.
items: Communication: Networking makes communication faster and easier by connecting people through email, instant messaging, video calls, and social media. It allows individuals and organizations to exchange information in real time, regardless of distance.

Resource Sharing: Networks allow multiple users to share resources such as printers, files, and applications. This reduces costs and improves efficiency since devices and data can be accessed by anyone connected to the network.

Data Access and Storage: Networking enables centralized data storage in servers or cloud systems. This makes information easier to manage, secure, and retrieve, ensuring that users can access the same updated data from different locations.

Collaboration: Through networking, teams can work together on shared platforms like Google Drive or Microsoft Teams. It supports group projects, online learning, and business operations by allowing multiple users to edit and access documents simultaneously.

slides.title: Characteristics of Computer Networking
slides.lead: Dependable networks protect sensitive data, remain consistently available, and scale as users grow.
items: Security: Networks must protect data from unauthorized access, hacking, and malware. Security features like firewalls, encryption, and authentication help safeguard sensitive information and ensure privacy.
Reliability: A reliable network ensures consistent availability of data and services. Backup systems and redundancy help maintain operations even during failures or disruptions.
Scalability: Scalable networks can grow by adding more devices or users without losing performance. This is essential for expanding businesses, schools, or online platforms.

slides.title: Four network coverage types
slides.lead: Network coverage classifies networks by their geographic scope: PAN, LAN, MAN, and WAN.
items: Personal Area Network (PAN): A tiny network within arm’s reach around one person—like a phone connected to wireless earbuds, a smartwatch, or a Bluetooth keyboard.
Local Area Network (LAN): Connects nearby computers, printers, and Wi-Fi devices inside one home, classroom, office, or school campus under local management.
Metropolitan Area Network (MAN): Links multiple buildings or branch offices together across a city or town, such as connecting city halls or public library branches.
Wide Area Network (WAN): Connects distant cities, regions, or countries using telecom provider lines. The global Internet is the largest WAN interconnecting millions of networks.

slides.title: Two network service architectures
slides.lead: Network architecture defines whether devices share resources directly as equals (peer-to-peer) or through a dedicated server (client-server).

Client-server: A dedicated server hosts shared files, websites, or user logins so many student or worker client devices can request services reliably in one place.

slides.title: Six network topologies
items: Star: Every device plugs into a central switch with its own cable. One broken wire disconnects only that single PC while the rest stay online.
Bus: Older design where all devices share one main backbone cable. A single cut or loose terminator brings down the entire network.
Ring: Devices connect end-to-end in a closed loop, passing data around the circle. One break stops traffic unless a backup ring exists.
Full mesh: Every device has a direct link to every other device. Very reliable with instant backup paths, though it uses lots of cables.
Tree: Joins multiple star switches in a branching hierarchy from a core root switch. Simple to expand, though an upper-link cut isolates a branch.
Hybrid: Mixes two or more layouts—such as connecting several classroom star switches together onto a fast building or campus backbone.

slides.title: Network Hub
slides.lead: A hub is a legacy multiport repeater that blindly copies every incoming electrical signal out every other port.
paragraphs: Instead of isolating connections, all ports on a hub share one electrical bus. Because a hub works strictly at the physical signal level, it cannot read MAC or IP addresses.
Any incoming bit is flooded out every other port, forcing devices to take turns and creating collisions as more computers share the hub—which is why modern LANs replace hubs with switches.

slides.title: Why Networking Standards Are Needed
slides.lead: Networking standards let hardware and software from different manufacturers communicate reliably using shared rules.
paragraphs: Without shared rules, devices from different brands could not understand one another. Standards allow multi-vendor compatibility and competition—much like USB lets keyboards, flash drives, and laptops from different companies work together.

Standards can be formal (approved by official bodies) or de facto (widely adopted by industry practice) and typically mature through three steps: specifying the problem, selecting the best solution, and gaining industry-wide acceptance.

slides.title: Layered Tasks: The Postal Mail Analogy
slides.lead: Layering splits one complex network delivery into smaller, specialized steps—just like sending and receiving a postal letter.
paragraphs: When you mail a letter, you write and seal it in an envelope (higher layers), the local post office sorts and addresses it (middle layers), and a carrier transports it physically across roads (lower layers). At the destination, the steps reverse until your friend opens and reads the letter.

Inside the OSI model, each layer only communicates directly with the layer immediately above and below it on the same computer, while logically matching the corresponding layer on the receiving computer.

slides.title: Seven OSI layer responsibilities
items: Application: Faces user software—web browsers and email apps use protocols like Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), Domain Name System (DNS), and Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) here.
Presentation: Translates data formats, compresses files, and encrypts messages (like HTTPS) so both ends read them.
Session: Starts, keeps open, and cleanly closes ongoing two-way conversations between applications.
Transport: Adds port numbers to reach the exact app on a host and optionally checks that no segments were lost.
Network: Stamps logical source and destination Internet Protocol (IP) addresses so routers can choose paths across separate networks.
Data Link: Packages data into frames with local hardware Media Access Control (MAC) addresses so switches deliver them on the same link.
Physical: Turns everything into raw 1s and 0s sent as voltage pulses, fiber light flashes, or radio waves.

Bits (Layer 1): Raw binary 1s and 0s sent physically over cables, optical glass fiber, or wireless Wi-Fi radio.

slides.title: Fiber-Optic Cable Construction and Types
slides.lead: Fiber-optic cables send light pulses through glass cores to span long distances without electrical interference.

slides.title: What Is an Internet Protocol Address?
slides.lead: An Internet Protocol (IP) address is a logical Layer 3 number that identifies a device and its network so routers can deliver packets to it.
paragraphs: Unlike a permanent physical Media Access Control (MAC) address burned into hardware, an IPv4 address is a logical Layer 3 identity assigned by network configuration so traffic can be routed across networks.

Each IPv4 address has 32 binary bits split into four 8-bit octets separated by dots (0–255 in decimal). Within each octet, bits carry binary place values of 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, and 1 (from 2⁷ down to 2⁰)—so 11000000 equals 128 + 64 = 192.

slides.title: Five IPv4 Address Classes (A–E) and Priority Bits
items: Class A (priority bit 0 · 0–127): Format N.H.H.H with default mask 255.0.0.0 (/8); supports 126 usable networks and 16,777,214 hosts each for huge networks.
Class B (priority bits 10 · 128–191): Format N.N.H.H with default mask 255.255.0.0 (/16); supports 16,384 networks and 65,534 hosts each for medium-to-large organizations.
Class C (priority bits 110 · 192–223): Format N.N.N.H with default mask 255.255.255.0 (/24); supports 2,097,152 networks and 254 hosts each for small LANs.
Class D (priority bits 1110 · 224–239): Reserved for multicast group traffic where one packet is delivered simultaneously to subscribed receivers.
Class E (priority bits 1111 · 240–255): Reserved for experimental testing, future standards research, and development rather than public host assignment.

slides.title: The Subnet Mask: The Dividing Boundary
slides.lead: A subnet mask uses binary 1s to lock in the network portion and binary 0s to mark the host portion.
paragraphs: Binary 1s lock in the network portion while binary 0s mark the host portion. In CIDR slash notation, /24 marks 24 network bits (255.255.255.0), /16 marks 16 (255.255.0.0), and /8 marks 8 (255.0.0.0).
Subtracting the prefix length from 32 gives the remaining host bits—so a /24 subnet leaves 8 host bits (254 usable device addresses).

slides.title: Inside Every Subnet: Network, Broadcast, and Host IPs
slides.lead: Every subnet reserves its first address as the Network ID, its last as the Broadcast IP, and the middle addresses for hosts.
paragraphs: The very first IP in a subnet is the Network ID (such as 192.168.1.0), which identifies the subnet itself, and the last IP is the Broadcast IP (such as 192.168.1.255), which delivers traffic to every host on that subnet. Neither may be assigned to a computer.

All middle addresses (.1 through .254 in a /24 block) are usable host IPs assigned to routers, servers, printers, and student workstations—giving the classic total-minus-two rule for usable host counts.

slides.title: Five Steps to Subnet a Network (With Example)
items: Step 1 — Count borrowed bits (2ⁿ ≥ subnets): Dividing 192.168.10.0/24 into 4 subnets needs n = 2 borrowed bits because 2² = 4.
Step 3 — Compute block size (256 − mask octet): 256 − 192 = 64 addresses per subnet, with 2⁶ − 2 = 62 usable hosts each.
Step 4 — List all subnet Network IDs: Increment the fourth octet by 64 → 192.168.10.0, .64, .128, and .192.
Step 5 — Identify usable host & broadcast ranges: Subnet 1 spans .0–.63 (hosts .1–.62, broadcast .63); Subnet 2 spans .64–.127 (hosts .65–.126, broadcast .127), continuing through .255.

slides.title: How Hosts Decide if a Peer is Local
slides.lead: Both computers must agree they are in the same subnet for a local request and its reply to succeed.
paragraphs: When two hosts share the same subnet mask and network prefix, they deliver frames directly through the switch without a router. When their network portions differ, traffic goes to the default gateway instead.
Because each host checks the mask independently, a mismatched mask causes one computer to treat its neighbor as local while the other tries to send replies to a router—breaking two-way connectivity.

slides.lead: A DHCP server lends each client a temporary IP address along with its subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS server.

slides.title: Four messages in the initial DHCP exchange
slides.lead: DHCP assigns an IP address in four steps called DORA: Discover, Offer, Request, and Acknowledgment.

Offer: A reachable DHCP server picks an unused IP from its pool and replies with an offer, mask, gateway, and DNS.
Request: The client answers publicly asking to accept that specific offered IP so any other servers know it chose this one.
Acknowledgment (ACK): The server records the active lease in its table and sends final confirmation so the client starts using the IP.

slides.title: DHCP Lease Lifecycle and Common Faults
slides.lead: Clients renew leases before they expire, release them when leaving, or fall back to 169.254.x.x if no server responds.
paragraphs: Each DHCP lease has a finite timer: healthy clients renew their lease before it runs out, return it early with a Release when shutting down cleanly, or allow it to expire so the server reclaims the IP for other devices.

slides.title: Six Windows diagnostic commands
slides.lead: Six built-in Windows commands—ipconfig, ipconfig /all, ping, tracert, nslookup, and arp -a—reveal where a connection is failing.
items: ipconfig: Quick check showing your PC’s active IPv4 address, subnet mask, and default gateway—great for spotting missing or APIPA settings.
ipconfig /all: Full network report adding your physical Media Access Control (MAC) address, which DHCP server gave your lease, when it expires, and DNS servers.
ping: Sends test Echo messages to an IP or name to verify basic reachability, packet loss, and round-trip speed in milliseconds.
tracert: Traces each router hop along the path so you can see exactly where distant packets slow down or stop.
nslookup: Asks your DNS server to look up a website name, separating naming failures from broken network cables or routing.
arp -a: Lists the local memory table pairing nearby Local Area Network (LAN) IP addresses with hardware MAC addresses found on your switch.

slides.title: Common Network Fault Symptoms
paragraphs: In practice, connectivity failures usually fall into physical link issues (an unplugged Ethernet cable or disconnected Wi-Fi client) or addressing errors (wrong static IP, mismatched subnet mask, duplicate IP conflict, or unavailable DHCP server resulting in APIPA).

Denial-of-Service (DoS): Overwhelming a website, router, or server with huge floods of fake traffic so normal users cannot connect.

items: CIA Triad: Confidentiality keeps data private, Integrity prevents tampering, and Availability keeps services online.
Four Major Threats: Malware infects hosts, phishing steals passwords, intrusions probe ports, and DoS floods servers.
Stateful Firewalls & TLS: Firewalls block unauthorized inbound probes, while HTTPS/TLS encrypts data in transit.
Human & Account Defense: Strong passwords, MFA, regular updates, and spotting phishing links stop most breaches.
